  Palos Verdes Estates Community Conversations
  Executive Summary
  This report summarizes the collaborative community engagement work done by the Davenport
  Institute with the City of Palos Verdes Estates. The Davenport Institute is a proud promoter and
  facilitator of deliberative community engagement for local governments.

  Project Background
  The primary reason Palos Verdes Estates reached out was to increase trust and
  communication between residents and City. After the failure of a parcel tax vote,
  city officials were left questioning whether the issue was one of misaligned
  service priorities, insufficient communication regarding the potential impact of a
  failed tax measure, or a lack of trust regarding how government management of
  resources and services. The City also sought perspectives and dialogue that may
  not be heard in traditional processes, and sought to build both internal and
  external knowledge and capacity for future engagement around substantive
  issues. The Davenport Institute is not an expert on issues specific to Palos Verdes
  Estates, but instead was tasked to design an engagement strategy tailored to
  building knowledge of resident priorities and capacity for civic engagement.

  Engagement can be defined by a range of processes from providing clear,
  dependable information to residents, through asking residents to choose between
  or prioritize pre-set options, to empowering them to participate in the
  development and delivery of local policies and services.

  For the purposes of this pilot effort, the Institute recommended that, before
  engaging residents toward the right end of the public engagement spectrum (for
  instance, around substantive decisions like budget prioritization or long-term
  planning), it was important to both model effective engagement and address the
  issue of trust by demonstrating the City’s willingness to listen. It was also
  important to ensure that the City’s engagement efforts aligned with the concerns
  of residents - that residents would not only feel heard but be heard.

Process
The engagement sessions used a World Café format. Participants initially self-
selected themselves into three groups, and were given twenty minutes to
discuss one question concerning the community, then a related follow-up
question concerning engagement. The groups were then jumbled and the
process was repeated two more times using different questions. Community
issues questions involved: why the resident chose PVE as a home, what services
and decisions residents expect from city, and concerns about PVE’s future.

Engagement follow-up questions included: how all members can contribute to
the community, how members would like to be personally involved, and how
residents would like to participate in decision-making. The groups were
moderated by Davenport Institute personnel and consultants to ensure
respectful dialogue that included all perspectives from those participants.

Findings
All four engagement sessions were lively and productive. The entirety of
responses and opinions were documented, then compiled. This process revealed
major themes that this report will detail and elaborate upon. A brief summary of
the findings is listed below:

  Participants highly value many characteristics of living in Palos Verdes
  Estates, especially the rural beauty found in its unique location. They also
  like the family-focused, friendly nature of their community (including
  school district). The community enjoys local control and values the work of
  city administrators.

  Participants expect various services from the city -- particularly police and
  fire. They want transparency and responsiveness in their city government,
  and above all, fiscal prudence. Retaining Palos Verdes Estates’ individual
  community identity (i.e. open spaces and rural feel) is a high priority for
  residents.

  Considering the recent budgetary issues, it comes as no surprise that a
  main concern is whether PVE will remain financially secure. Other concerns
  included: loss of local control, “mansionification,” aging demographics,
  preserving parkland, traffic, vitriol in the community, and interaction
  between the City, Planning Commission, and Homes Assn.

  Participants prioritized community engagement moving forward, as
  residents approved of the “Community Conversations,” and want be
  involved in questions relating to the budget. They also voiced their desire
  for more, and increased clarity communications from the city. Participants
  expressed their willingness to help, especially in possible informal
  community building opportunities (get-togethers).

  Report: Palos Verdes Estates Community Conversations
  Overview
  This report outlines the purpose, facilitation, and key findings of a series of public engagement workshops
  (Community Conversations) commissioned by the City Council and conducted pro-bono by the Davenport
  Institute for Public Engagement and Civic Leadership. It also offers some recommendations for next steps the
  City may want to consider as it pursues stronger resident engagement.

  About the Davenport Institute
  The Davenport Institute for Public Engagement and Civic Leadership at the Pepperdine School of
  Public Policy is a non-partisan, not-for-profit organization committed to helping build stronger
  communities in California by promoting public participation in local governance. We work with
  local governments, nonprofit organizations, and residents to both promote and support
  constructive and broad-based civic involvement in decisions that affect people where they live
  and work.

  We work in partnership with professional dialogue facilitators. For the purpose of this project we
  worked with Janine Hamner, the co-founder and CEO of J&J Consulting Group, LLC. Ms. Hamner
  brought more than 30 years of meeting facilitation, organizational development and community
  engagement and outreach experience to the project. She was a senior manager for non-profit
  organizations and a public affairs and community engagement manager for Waste Management
  before creating her own consulting firm.

  Commitment to Participatory Local Government
  The Davenport Institute strives to be a champion of public engagement as a 21st Century leadership skill
  for governments and residents to succeed together in an age where California’s communities face fiscal
  constraints, difficult land use decisions, environmental challenges, and changing demographics. The 21st
  Century is also a time of increased polarization and of decreased trust in many public institutions (not
  just government). In this context deliberation is both more important and more challenging than ever.

  The City of Palos Verdes Estates reached out to the Institute for help engaging with residents beyond
  the traditional city council meeting or public hearing with its formal agenda and 3-minutes at a mic
  public comment. We advised the City that good public engagement requires residents to engage not
  only with government but also with each other in the difficult work of self-governance.

  In early conversations with City council and staff, the City identified increasing trust between the City
  and its residents as the key purpose for engagement. This conclusion arose from two concerns. The first
  of these was the failure of the parcel tax to receive the necessary ⅔ majority vote, which seemed to
  suggest a misalignment of either priorities  (did residents in fact want fewer services?), trust (did

  02Determines Process
 Purpose
When it comes to public engagement, there is no one-size-fits-all solution. Rather, public engagement
encompasses a spectrum of activities, with the appropriate activity determined by the purpose of the
engagement. The Davenport Institute draws on the International Association of Public Participation’s
(IAP2) “Spectrum of Public Engagement” (see Appendix 2 for a more comprehensive explanation of the
IAP2 Spectrum).

Each stage of this spectrum comprises the next. As public engagement activities move from the left to
the right side of the spectrum - that is from communication and transparency to sophisticated
deliberative exercises to actual co-delivery of services and sharing of policy development - different
processes are required.

A traditional Q&A set up with community members seated auditorium style and staff or council sharing
from the front of the room may, in fact, be perfectly sufficient for an information session about how
new state mandates will affect city water usage, for example. However, this type of room setup cannot
facilitate the sort of dialogue and creative collaboration needed for more deliberative engagement. For
this kind of engagement, processes that encourage dialogue and even disagreement among participants
become key.

About the Community Conversations
As noted, this effort has, in many ways, been a first foray into deliberative public engagement for the
City of Palos Verdes Estates. The Institute recommended that, before engaging residents toward the right
end of the public engagement spectrum (for instance, around substantive decisions like budget
prioritization or long-term planning), it was important to address the issue of trust by demonstrating the
City’s willingness to listen. It was also important to ensure that the City’s engagement efforts aligned
with the concerns of residents - that residents would not only feel heard but be heard.

For this reason, we recommended a series of “Community Conversations” that involved residents sharing
with each other their values, priorities, and concerns about the community. For this effort City council
and staff would be present only to listen. The purpose of these conversations was to identify areas for
deeper engagement as well as to provide a taste of what a more deliberative process can look like in
Palos Verdes Estates, and equip staff with new engagement skills. The value of the pilot will largely
depend on what the City does with the feedback received. Some recommendations for next steps can be
found at the end of this report.

Working with the City, and with generous accommodation from the school district, we determined to
hold four workshops in different parts of the City:
  5:30 - 7 pm on Thursday, October 12 (Montemalaga Elementary School)
  9- 11 am on Saturday October 14 (Lunada Bay Elementary School)
  6-8 pm on Monday, October 16 (Valmonte Early Learning School)
  6-8 pm on Wednesday, October 18 (PVUPSD at Malaga Cove School)
Outreach and Participation
Outreach regarding the meetings took place through all of the usual public noticing means,
including the City website & social media, E-newsletter, and regular newsletter. The City also posted
physical banners on major thoroughfares, posted notification in City Hall locations, sponsored
boosted posts on Facebook, and provided postcard and email invitations to council to send to
constituents. It is important to note the value of personal, individualized invitations, especially for
new efforts where residents may not know what to expect. The City asked the school district to
distribute info via email and flyers, and distributed flyers to local homeowners associations, citizens
academy, and city volunteers.
   6
Altogether, the four meetings drew a turnout of about 100 residents. While this number may seem
small in terms of percentage of population, it actually represents a very good turnout for a first foray
into deliberative processes. Especially in the early days of engagement efforts, the Davenport
Institute encourages cities to look at the quality of the conversation over the number of participants.
We are often brought into contexts where the relationship between council and the public is not
seen as very inclusive. This new type of deliberation- open to everyone and communicated through
a variety of outlets - sends a message even to those who were not present. What we are looking at is
nothing less than culture change for both City officials and residents: redefining what is possible in a
relationship with the City. Such change takes time, effort, and demonstrated commitment.

Ultimately, when it comes to engagement, citizens have a choice of how engaged they will be. Nor
can too much be assumed about those who did not participate, as opting out may be a sign of
apathy, contentment, or simply a very full calendar.

From conversations that we had with residents who participated, it was obvious that many (though
not all) of them have sought to actively engage with the City in the past. Both participants and City
Council and staff expressed concerns regarding those who were not in the room and a desire for
greater diversity of participation. This is a goal City staff and residents should continue to strive for
and one they can partner on.

100 self-selected people is obviously not a representative sample, and the issues and concerns
identified in the community conversations may or may not reflect those of the broader community.
Of course, that is also true of a city council meeting or public hearing. The advantage in a more
deliberative process is the opportunity to have a significantly more positive and productive
conversation with those who do participate.

In a process like this, even the “usual attendees” do not have a usual experience in their interactions
with government or each other. In many ways, those who did show up represent a core group that
can become a network and ambassadors to the rest of the community. If they appreciated the
process, and if the City closes the loop by incorporating their feedback into future engagement
efforts around substantive policy issues, participation will become broader, but only if the City
embraces an ongoing commitment to engagement.

Observations and Lesson Learned
The turnout for the Community Conversations was better than typical for a first deliberative effort
in a small city, and we learned some valuable lessons that may help to inform planning and
outreach for future engagement:
  Framing: Initially we called the Community Conversations “Community Conversations for PVE at
  100.” The thought behind this was a) to connect them to the identity of the community and b)
  to signal that this was the first of multiple engagements. However many people were confused
  by what sounded like a conversation about something twenty years in the future. Lesson = be
  simple and concrete in framing so that people know what to expect.

  Timeline: Because we did not want these conversations to be confused with either the police
  study or efforts around the parcel tax, we ended up fitting all 4 workshops in the span of a week.
  Ideally, spreading meetings out over the course of several weeks would accommodate residents
  who may be out of town or simply overbooked. We would recommend a longer time frame for
  engagement in the future.
  (continued next page)
   7
  Saturday  meetings are good, but avoid Monday night: While many residents with young
  families have sports or other commitments on Saturday morning, we had good turnout and
  energy on Saturday and recommend a Saturday time slot for future efforts. While turnout on
  Monday night was only slightly lower than on other nights, the energy in the room was
  significantly diminished. People may have been tired from the weekend without yet being back
  in the swing of work. We did not have a weekday morning meeting, but it may be interesting to
  try that in the future to see what kind of participation it would attract.

  A few (2-3) people attended multiple meetings: They chose to do so either because they had an
  issue of particular concern that they wanted addressed in every meeting, or else simply out of
  curiosity regarding how the process differed in different neighborhoods. While this again
  demonstrates why such workshops should not be taken as a referendum of resident opinion,
  those who attended multiple times did have the opportunity to engage with different groups of
  neighbors each time. We in no way discouraged people from engaging as often as they wanted.
  We suspect future engagement efforts may also draw a couple of people to multiple events.

  About the Community Conversations
  As noted above, because our purpose was to build trust and break down a perception that
  residents were not being consistently heard by the City, we recommended a process that would
  invite participants to engage with each other while City Council and staff simply observed. Because
  the Community Conversations were about resident priorities rather than about particular policies,
  there was no need for City involvement even in presenting information, defining constraints or
  answering questions (all of which may be a perfectly legitimate part of future public engagement
  efforts).

  Participants were also asked to agree to ground rules, and neutral facilitators (Davenport Institute
  staff and partners) were empowered to enforce these ground rules. It is worth noting that while
  facilitators did step in to make sure quieter residents’ voices were heard, or to remind residents that
  they should not engage staff or council, all participants took ownership of the ground rules and
  engaged in the conversation in good will.

Key Findings
Appendix 1 contains a categorized compilation of all comments received in the 4 community
workshops. While we encourage City Council and staff to review all comments in order to
grasp the full scope of the Community Conversations, this report will highlight some key
findings:

What Participants Value: It is probably not a surprise to the City that much of what
participants most value about living in Palos Verdes Estates relates to the natural beauty
and rural nature of the community. Participants do not mind that PVE is out of the way;
they value the parklands, trails, lack of light pollution and air pollution, and historic
architecture. Other things that came up as frequent themes include:

  Participants value the family-focus and overall friendliness of the community: They
  like living in a place where kids can ride their bikes or explore trails in relative safety
  and independence. Interestingly, comments about how great PVE teens are came up
  more than once.
  Participants place a high priority on local control: This was a consistent response in all
  three small group conversations at every meeting. Residents value and expect local
  control, particularly of police and fire, and desire the City to receive enough funding to
  maintain or even expand current levels of service. A few expressed interest in
  understanding the tradeoffs of a contract more clearly, even though they wanted the City
  to maintain its own police department. The importance of keeping “our own” police force
  and fire department was a key concern in the financial discussion as well. But interest in
  local control was not limited to public safety. Residents also expressed concerns about
  things like the impact of state mandates on local self-determination, and the impact of
  surrounding communities on PVE identity.
  Participants value and appreciate their City Government and Administration: This is
  something City staff and council may not be used to hearing frequently, but a number of
  participants noted that they think their government does a good job, particularly
  compared to other cities.
  Participants value education and the local school district: Although not directly related to
  city government, this came up frequently in answer to the question “what brought you
  here” - though some participants also expressed concern that standards of education in
  PVE may be slipping, and noted they would like to be more involved and engaged with the
  school district as well as the city.

What Participants Expect from the City: It is important to note here (particularly for anyone
digging into the appendix) that this question did not assume that the City is delinquent in
providing these services. Most participants seemed to think the City is doing a good job of
providing many of the services listed. Exceptions to that are captured in the discussion of
concerns. Much of what this conversation elicited were basic “role of local” government
responses - public works, infrastructure, maintenance, etc. The appendix lists these
comprehensively, but we will highlight a few of the most frequent themes here:

  Police and Fire Services: Although noted above, this came up frequently enough as
  something that people expect and receive from the city that it should be mentioned
  here. One interesting comment that came up in this conversation was “they know us
  and we know them” as an important benefit to having one’s own police department.
  Transparency and Information relating to both financial and regulatory information
   9
  Responsiveness: Participants want responses to complaints and inquiries, but they also
  want to be engaged in decision-making (more on that below).
  Retaining Community Identity and Open Space: Many participants commented on
  maintaining open space and parklands, while others noted the important role the city
  plays in regulation of development, including the historic CCRs
  Good Fiscal Management/ Balanced Budget

What Participants are Concerned About: It is interesting - and important - to note how many
of the items that residents raised as concerns were about losing the things they listed as
important about the community. In particular:
  Participants are concerned about the City’s future given its current financial situation:
  With the failure of the parcel tax, participants were concerned about ensuring the
  financial security of the City, especially related to the services they rely upon. Most
  participants seemed surprised the tax hadn’t passed, and saw it as a sign of apathy or
  ignorance rather than opposition. Some offered to campaign for a future tax measure.
  Participants are concerned about losing local control: Again, this was a theme
  throughout- as a value, an expectation, and something people are afraid of losing.
  Participants are concerned about mansionification and maintaining the rural nature of
  the community: This was another very common theme, related to participant values of
  community identity and history. Some residents also commented on the impact of
  residential building and expansion projects in their neighborhood (traffic, noise, etc).
  Participants are concerned about what it means to be an aging community: Participants
  were well aware that PVE skews older in its demographics, and were interested in what
  that would mean for the future of the City, as well in what it would look like for residents
  to be able to age in place.
  Participants are concerned about park lands: Certainly among those who attended the
  workshops, the issue about sale of park lands and ensuing lawsuit are still quite raw.
  Some acknowledged that there have been changes in leadership since then, but
  expressed concern about management of park lands in the future. Given this history, and
  the value that residents place on open space, trails, etc. this issue is likely to remain one
  that requires extra efforts at engagement in order to build trust.
  Traffic is a major concern for many participants, particularly the way that PVE traffic is
  impacted by development in surrounding communities. Several noted that they know this
  isn’t something the City can control, and that they appreciate that the City advocates for
  them when it can.
  Participants are concerned about increased polarization/ vitriol within the community:
  Many saw this exacerbated by social media platforms like NextDoor, but felt that the level
  of incivility extended beyond that. From our experience in the public engagement world,
  this is a national theme that is reflected in many communities. Related to this was a
  concern about where to go for trustworthy information. Participants recognize the threat
  of “fake news” but don’t know who to trust or where to look to obtain good information.
  Participants are concerned about interactions between the City, the Planning
  Commission, and the Homes Association. There is a desire that the various players make
  decisions that are consistent with each other and with historic guidelines. There also
  seemed to be uncertainty about the role that each played and concern that guidelines
  were not clear enough to be equitably enforced (or perhaps that they had been enforced
  unequally and so become less clear).
What Participants Said about Engagement with the City: Engagement was discussed as a subset
of each group. For that reason much of the feedback on questions 2, 4, and 6 in appendix 1
overlap. While we recommend that Council and staff take the time to explore those in detail,
we here offer some key observations.
   10
  Participants appreciate the effort demonstrated in the Community Conversations and
  desired more opportunities for creative, positive engagement. A frequent theme was a
  desire for more informal dialogue both between community members and between
  community members and key staff and council. Many noted that they want to be engaged
  but that council meetings feel negative or intimidating and they would like more dialogue
  beyond the 3 minutes at a microphone. They are interested in more open and “safer”
  formats - perhaps around specific areas of concern.
  Participants want to be engaged in decisions around the budget/finances and in
  discussion of trade offs between budget and services. What this should look like ranged
  from a simple desire for more accessible and understandable information, to workshops
  and dialogue around trade offs (this was by far the most common way people suggested
  being involved) to a citizens' oversight committee (which two participants advocated for).
  Participants desire more and clearer information from the City: This ranged from better
  information around budgets, to closing the loop on decisions that are made at council
  meetings, to providing more clarity around guidelines and codes. Several noted that it is
  difficult to get useful information from meeting agendas and meeting minutes, and they
  often don’t know what decisions are made following an inquiry, discussion, or council
  meeting. There was a wide divergence of opinions about how that might work better.
  Participants desire greater diversity in participation: They acknowledged that young
  families and young people in general were underrepresented and discussed strategies that
  both they and the City could undertake to both get more people to the table, and perhaps
  to bring the table to more people (including using existing events or online opportunities).
  Participants are interested in helping and supporting the City with their talents and don’t
  know how to do it. The conversation about donating money to the City came up more than
  once and there were many who expressed willingness to volunteer specific skills or time
  and wanting to know how to plug into the City - in addition to genuinely wanting to know
  what the City needs/ can use from its residents.
  Participants are interested in online opportunities for engagement. They were also wary of
  things like public comment on a website or social media and many had been burned by
  NextDoor. They are anxious for more creative deliberative online engagement.
  Participants believe that residents had an obligation to commit to civility.
  Participants are also interested in informal community building opportunities. Things like
  summer concerts, the school community garden and other productive relationship-building
  opportunities were things they felt they could take ownership of, as well as help the City to
  support.

Observations and Lesson Learned
It was sometimes a challenge to encourage participants to identify how 'they' would personally
be involved, and the discussion often turned into ways to find other people to get involved. A
few people were straightforward enough to say they didn't want to be involved much (even
though they had come to the workshop). This raises the valid objection that many citizens are
too busy to participate. Still, by far, the majority of people identified at least a couple of issues
in which they wanted to be involved, and several people felt they would be more willing to be
involved if they were convinced it would have an effect/impact. This demonstrates that the
opportunity to engage may be as important in its own way as actual participation and highlights
why it is important not to rely on numbers of participants as the sole measure of success.
 Recommendations for Next Steps
  11

As we have already noted, the success of this first foray into public engagement will largely
be determined by what the City does with the information it has received. The first and most
important step the City can take is to ensure that residents know how feedback is being used.
It is essential that City Council follow up on these conversations with a discussion of the
results - preferably in an informal or non-traditional format. This will demonstrate that the
council takes community feedback seriously and is committed to acting on the major themes.
It will also provide an opportunity to create buy-in for future community engagement efforts
and to begin to spread the word about what some of those might be.

We here offer some ideas for further steps, emphasizing that improving public engagement
involves shifting the culture within both the City and the community. There is no one-size-
fits all model for culture change, nor is it something that can be accomplished in one fell
swoop. The suggestions below should be considered and prioritized in light of council and
staff capacity, budget constraints, and other factors.

The City of Rancho Palos Verdes Estates may choose to:

Council Policy on Public Engagement that defines public engagement and sets guidelines for

of one or more staff members in order to ensure that it remains a city priority, and commit to
further training for staff and council on effective civic engagement. Debrief and evaluate
current and future engagement efforts for lessons learned and insights into engagement in

   Engage
  12  with residents outside City Hall on issues that were identified as important to those who
  participated in the Community Conversations: We demonstrated one of a variety of many
  deliberative formats. The appropriate format for future engagement will be largely
  determined by the issue under consideration. In this format there was no opportunity for
  interaction with City Council or staff. In other contexts it can be completely appropriate for
  City representatives to set the stage by providing information about issues and constraints
  before deliberation takes place, or even for answering questions during deliberation. Again, in
  the public engagement spectrum, each step comprises those that come before it. It is
  impossible to have good collaboration without solid information.

  However as soon as you move beyond the “informing” step, there are two key elements to
  any good engagement process:

  1. Residents should have an opportunity to discuss matters in facilitated small group
  discussions. Not every issue requires an outside consultant. The City may want to
  provide training to key staff in order to be able to facilitate some conversations
  internally. It should also have a strategy for identifying issues where past experience or
  current political context make outside facilitation expedient.
  2. The City should be clear about what level of input it is asking for and what options are
  or are not on the table. The City should clearly define constraints and should not
  advocate for any particular outcome within those constraints.
  The Davenport Institute, as well as organizations such as the Institute for Local Government
  and the International Association of Public Participation provide a variety of trainings on the
  elements of good engagement, and have a variety of case studies available to demonstrate
  how different organizations have undertaken deliberative processes. We would be happy to
  connect the City of Palos Verdes Estates with any of these resources.

  Expand the City's commitment to transparency by putting more information on the website in easily
  navigable and understandable formats: A key concern from residents of PVE (and also reflected
  in the national dialogue) is the challenge of knowing where to go for good information in an
  age of social media and false news. To fill this gap, local governments must go well beyond the
  minimum requirements of transparency. There are excellent budget visualization tools
  available to cities at low-cost. Also consider the use of infographics and illustrations for non-
  financial information.

  Continue to experiment with ways to expand attendance and increase the diversity of
  participation: Participants mentioned that they appreciated things like coffee with the mayor -
  it may be valuable to hold such informal meetings and/or focus groups on key issues. The City
  may want to host tables at community events where you can both provide information to
  residents and also allow residents to share their views about issues in safe, respectful dialogue.
  The City may want to seek ways to get on the agendas of service groups, HOAs, and civic clubs
  and organizations in order to provide updates and answer questions. Surveys may also be
  helpful for taking the pulse of the broad community, though they have significant limitations,
  particularly when it comes to deliberation.
  Build on the community pride evident in the Community Conversations: Participants appreciate
  opportunities together informally and get to know one another. The City may want to think
  creatively about how to foster celebrations of the many reasons PVE is such a desirable place
  to live and raise a family.

The Davenport Institute has a menu of trainings and resources available to California cities. We are
happy to consider how we might partner with PVE in the future, or how we may connect the City to
strategic partners who can help build upon this City Council's commitment to resident engagement.

  Recommendations

  Given these results, this report offers several recommendations regarding
  next steps for community engagement in Palos Verdes Estates. Most
  significantly, the City must close the loop on this pilot process, so that
  residents know how feedback is being incorporated and are made aware of
  future engagement plans. What those plans may be will be dependent on
  Council, staff, and budget capacity, but may include some of the following:

  1. Instituting public engagement as part of how the City does business,
  through development of an official public engagement policy or strategy, the
  assignment of engagement as a part of key staff job descriptions, and a
  commitment to ongoing public engagement training for staff and
  council.

  2. Creatively experimenting with online deliberation - beyond social media
  presence and website Q&A pages, the city should seek ways to offer
  constructive deliberation online.

  3. Seeking to to engage with residents outside of City Hall on issues that were
  identified as important to those who participated in the Community
  Conversations. Further interactions should be strategically designed towards
  deliberative dialogue.

  4. Increasing transparency and dispelling false information by putting more
  information (financial, operational, and issue-focused) on the website in
  easily navigable and understandable formats.

  5. Continuing to experiment with ways to expand and increase the diversity
  of participation through formal and informal, online and offline processes
  and strategic partnerships.

  6. Lastly, the residents of Palos Verdes Estates exhibited considerable
  community pride during the “Community Conversations.” Harnessing this
  pride is crucial in benefitting the community.

  The following report provides more details as to how these efforts can be
  accomplished, and the Davenport Institute would be happy to discuss further
  support we may be able to provide to the City through our own training and
  consultation as well as through partnerships with others in the public
  engagement field.

This memo outlines some options and associated costs should the City of Palos Verdes Estates
choose to continue to work with the Davenport Institute on future public engagement efforts.

From the questions that Councilmembers asked at the November 14 meeting, it is clear that
there is interest in how exactly the City can match process to purpose. When is a “listening” only
session appropriate? When should council or staff provide more information or answer
questions? What might this type of engagement look like? On what issues is an outside
facilitator necessary? When should the City be able to “go it alone”?

To answer these questions, the Davenport Institute offers a range of trainings, consultation, and
facilitation. These are outlined below, with associated pricing.

Training
Option 1: Half-Day Training. The Davenport Institute could offer a four hour training for City
staff (and interested members of council) on the basics of public engagement. This training
would be tailored to PVE and would encourage conversations about what to do next and various
styles of community meetings. It would also build on the lessons learned from the initial
Community Conversations. We would include examples of city policies adopted by other
jurisdictions, ways cities make policy and performance data more readable and accessible on
their websites, and samples of job description language regarding public engagement
responsibilities.

The City would receive all training materials and the PowerPoint for future reference. The
training would be conducted by two trainers (most likely myself and Davenport Institute Sr.
Fellow Rod Gould, who I know has conducted workshops with council on other issues).
Cost: $2,800

Option 2: Full Day - Training + Workshop. This option would include the training outlined
above, but would include an additional four hours of workshop where staff would actually design
community meetings on specific topics. There would be opportunities for basic facilitation
training with role play. Participants would also discuss what issues may require outside
facilitation for historical or political reasons, and what issues staff would feel confident facilitating
internally. Participants would walk away with rough outlines for engagement, and the ability to
conduct some public workshops on issues where outside facilitation is not necessary.

The City would be expected to provide lunch for participants. This training would be open to all
staff and Council. Cost: $4,800
 Public Workshops
Should the City Council identify a specific topic on which it would like to next engage the public,
the Davenport Institute is happy to design and facilitate meetings if needed. Meeting and
Materials Design Cost: $600 per topic (This is a baseline price - some complex topics may
require more prep work. This would be charged at $150/ hour based on an estimate submitted
before we begin the work). Meeting facilitation: $150 per hour (most workshops will require
only one facilitator, plus help from city staff and a graduate assistant, but certain topics and
workshop designs may require an additional facilitator at the same rate)

Because the Davenport Institute is not-for-profit, we are able to offer a discounted rate to local
governments. We also are near enough to PVE that travel costs are not an issue. Should we
need to refer the City to an outside facilitator for capacity reasons, rates run $200-$350/ hour.

Online Engagement
The Davenport Institute is not a tech firm, so we cannot provide a platform of online
engagement. We do offer a half-day training to help staff and Council navigate the expansive
world of Gov 2.0 and to develop a framework for determining which platform(s) are best suited
to their purpose. The cost for this training is the same as for the other half day training ($2,800)
and again is open to all staff and Council, and the City receives materials, examples, and
powerpoint.

Regarding the cost of online engagement itself, the price can vary widely - some platforms have
simple pricing structures ($2K per project for examples) while others price according to the size
of the community or the complexity of the project. If the City identifies particular issues it would
like to engage residents around, the Davenport Institute would be happy to consult on what
platform may be best suited to your needs. Our consulting rate would be $150/hr.

As mentioned at the City Council meeting, David Fridley is willing to work with PVE for free
using his platform. He also seems willing to work with the City to customize that platform. While
the Davenport Institute does not endorse specific platforms, this seems like a good opportunity
to “get your feet wet,” especially if you are able to work with him to get a product that works for
you.

Consultation - Preparing for and Promoting Engagement
Finally we would be happy to host a brainstorming session with staff and/or Council about how
to engage a broader cross section of the PVE public, including how you might market
engagement, getting on established groups’ agendas for presentations and feedback, what
existing events (both city and community sponsored) you may be able to host pop-up tables or
games at and what new events you may want to undertake. Again, the consulting rate would be
$150/ hr. We are also happy to connect you with consultants who may have more specific
expertise in social media advertising, “tactical urbanism” or other creative community-building
efforts. We would not charge for these match-making efforts, but the price would vary according
to the consultant.
 I hope this helps guide your strategy conversation. I am happy to put together a formal proposal
with detailed pricing on any options that you would like to follow up on further.
